#5341. Portland startup Fairly raises $22M to pair local caretakers with AI for vacation rentals

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the company announced Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

Fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

Guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the company said. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the company says other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

“At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon said in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”

Breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The company went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The company has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the company in February.

#5340. ‘70% chance’ we’re already in an AI bubble: The economist who said ‘not yet’ in January now sees all four horsemen of the bubble apocalypse

Owen Lamont told Fortune in January that the stock market wasn’t in an AI bubble. Now he’s mostly convinced.

“I think there is a 70% chance that as of November 2026 we are already in an AI bubble in the U.S. stock market,” Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management and a former University of Chicago finance professor, told Fortune in an email. “I think a lot has changed this year.”

What changed is the one signal he used to say was missing. Lamont tracks what he calls the “four horsemen of the bubble apocalypse”: overvaluation, bubble beliefs, issuance and inflows of new money. At the time, he said three were present. The holdout was issuance, meaning companies selling new stock to the public. Back then, U.S. firms had bought back roughly $1 trillion of their own shares over the past year, and Lamont treats corporate executives as the “smart money.” They weren’t selling.

They are now. U.S. companies issued a net $2.4 trillion of stock over the 12 months to Nov. 12, by Lamont’s count. In the 12 months to November 2025, they bought back a net $69 billion, and a year before that, $397 billion. In his latest Owenomics blog post, he walks back his January headline: “Today, I would no longer write those words.”

“I think we basically have all four horsemen now,” he told Fortune.

The big number has a big asterisk. Of the $2.4 trillion issuance, $2.2 trillion comes from SpaceX’s June IPO, which Lamont’s method counts at its full market value. Strip it out and net issuance is $192 billion.

That’s still a reversal from net buybacks a year earlier, and the turn includes the biggest names: the Magnificent Seven went from net buybacks of $144 billion in the year to November 2024 to net issuance of $276 billion now, according to Lamont. He writes that Alphabet and Meta switched from buying back shares to issuing them, Tesla sharply increased issuance, and Meta announced plans to raise nearly $98 billion in equity to fund its AI spending.

Lamont admits the SpaceX question is “tough.” “I think one company is not enough to constitute a ‘wave of issuance,’” he said. “On the other hand, we live in a world of concentrated stock markets where a handful of companies have huge market cap, so maybe we should expect waves of issuance that are also concentrated.”

Professional investors are moving the other way: fund managers just cut their net overweight in tech to 12% from 37%, the biggest one-month drop since June 2006, according to Bank of America’s November survey.

Why companies are selling is the open question. In his note, Lamont laid out two explanations: “the smart money is selling because the market is overpriced,” or firms “need to fund the AI buildout.” Asked which he leans toward, he said: “I’m not sure. Could be both.”

Either way, the shares are going to someone. TD Securities’ rates strategists flagged the same shift from the bond side this week, noting that Meta and Oracle have issued equity and that more AI capex funded with stock could ease pressure on long-term Treasury yields.

He also thinks the case for overvaluation got stronger this year because real long-term interest rates rose about 100 basis points. But he isn’t calling a top. “It is not a slam dunk case: the market might be overvalued, but it is not absurdly overvalued,” he said. “Net issuance has turned positive, but it’s not strongly positive.”

By his measure, net issuance is running at 3.1% of total market value, still below the peaks of the 1999–2000 tech bubble and the 2021 COVID boom.

Lamont gave Fortune three conditions that would take him from 70% to a flat call.

“First, the Anthropic IPO occurs and is a success. Second, we see a wave of smaller IPOs, similar to what we saw in 2021: hundreds of IPOs, say five IPOs a week, many of them doubling on the first day. Third, CAPE ratio or other valuation ratios blow through prior records.”

The second one is far off. The U.S. had 90 IPOs in 2025, against 311 in 2021 and 677 in 1996, according to Jay Ritter’s data cited in Lamont’s March note. In January, he told Fortune the shortage of IPOs was “baffling,” and that a full bubble could look like the Nasdaq 100 doubling in a year with the Shiller CAPE ratio near 80. It was around 40 then.

The first condition is about a day away. Anthropic is set to price its IPO Wednesday and begin trading on Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT. Lamont writes that the deal, if it goes ahead, would push issuance above its 2021 peak. Asked if that’s the moment to watch, he said yes, and pointed back to his three conditions.

#5339. Meta is pausing issuance of non-voting stock while shareholders challenge the plan in court

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The charter creating the new class takes effect Jan. 19 under the filing, and a proposed schedule sets a trial for April

Photo by Laurent Hou/Hans Lucas /AFP via Getty Images

Meta $META Platforms said it will not issue any Class C stock, through a dividend or otherwise, while shareholder lawsuits over its reclassification plan are pending in Delaware. The company made the commitment in a stipulation filed Wednesday in the Delaware Court of Chancery.

The stipulation needs approval from Chancellor Kathaleen St. Jude McCormick. It sets trial for April 19-23, 2027, in Wilmington, and Meta's response to the consolidated complaint is due Nov. 24. Defendants say they do not expect the trial to need all five days.

The court consolidated the shareholder cases on Nov. 6 and named California State Teachers' Retirement System and PFA Pension forsikringsaktieselskab as lead plaintiffs, according to the filing. The 10 lawsuits allege that CEO Mark Zuckerberg and other board members breached their fiduciary duties, according to Bloomberg.

The filing says nothing in the order prevents the amended charter that creates the new class from taking effect Jan. 19, 2027. If a final, non-appealable order declares the charter invalid, Meta must file certificates of correction with the Delaware Secretary of State stating that it has been rescinded. The same step would apply to the certificate of designations for Meta's 6.50% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock, the filing says.

"In the best interest of our shareholders, we are seeking a final determination as quickly as the court will allow, and we will vigorously defend against these claims," Meta said in a statement, according to Bloomberg.

Meta had sought a fast-tracked trial, while the plaintiffs wanted McCormick to allow more time before the case is heard, according to Bloomberg. Meta has said it needs the new class to fund its AI infrastructure buildout and must act quickly, citing companies' loss of access to the bond market.

Meta's board approved the new non-voting class in October after a special committee made up of independent directors with no stake in the deal unanimously recommended it. The board declared a one-time dividend of one Class C share for each Class A and Class B share, contingent on the charter taking effect. The board will set the record and payment dates by later action, the company said.

Under an agreement with Meta, 20% of the Class C stock Zuckerberg receives would be freely saleable, and the other 80% would carry sale restrictions, according to the company's filing.

#5338. Radian Aerospace plans to make its own composite materials for space plane (and for other companies, too)

by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:00 am

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it plans to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey said he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems.

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

Humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

“Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey said today in a news release. “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”

Ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

Carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The company says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

Artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey said. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”

Greg Scofield, an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, said Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034.

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

Radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small company.

Humphrey said the company currently has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. Back in 2022, Radian announced a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

So, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey said. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”

He acknowledged that following through on the plan for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he said.

Humphrey said the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the company’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

“It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he said. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”

Is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace company? Humphrey said that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he said. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. It’s just the way I’ve come to accept it.”

#5337. Skilled trades leaders admit ‘nothing is future-proof’—but AI can’t replace America’s growing demand for blue-collar workers like auto technicians

As AI forces office workers to rethink how tasks get done, skilled trades jobs have largely been seen as a more insulated, safer path to a six-figure career. However, hands-on roles like plumbers, electricians, and auto technicians aren’t exactly immune to the changes sweeping the workforce, either.

“Nothing is future-proof,” Mary Culler, president of Ford Philanthropy, said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Summit on Tuesday. “But I do think that a lot of the skilled trades are just those jobs that are going to be required to have a human there.”

Auto technicians—who are in short supply, for example —could increasingly use AI to help diagnose vehicle problems, she said, but still need a human to do the actual manual labor.

Carhartt CEO Linda Hubbard echoed that AI-powered efficiency will change how skilled trades workers do their jobs—but she said that the industry’s labor needs—fueled by the data center boom and broader infrastructure investments—will continue to outpace any productivity gains from the technology.

“No matter how good we get at encouraging people, I think we’re always going to be challenged to get the number of people that we need into the trades to just rebuild the infrastructure of the country,” Hubbard said on stage in an interview with Fortune’s Kristin Stoller.

Employers are expected to fill approximately 1.7 million skilled trades openings annually between now and 2034—but roughly a quarter of the industry’s existing 18 million workers are over 55 and nearing retirement.

Skilled trades work isn’t for everyone. The jobs can be physically demanding, require working outdoors in difficult conditions, and sometimes depend on project availability. But they can also offer something increasingly attractive to workers: relatively strong job security, salaries that can reach six figures, and even a pathway to owning a business.

Getting more people to recognize those opportunities, however, has been a challenge.

“We’re seeing pushback both on the cost of college, what jobs really require college degrees,” said Maria Flynn, CEO of Jobs for the Future. But decades of trade policies and other economic shifts have also left some communities with fewer skilled trades opportunities than they once had, she said.

“We’re having to rebuild trust, rebuild that awareness, and helping parents, young people, school counselors really understand what these 124 different skilled trades occupations offer and what the paths are into those roles,” Flynn said.

That perception gap is particularly evident among the people responsible for advising students on their next steps. While 95% of counselors agree trade school is a valuable and credible post-high school option, just 54% say they often recommend vocational or trade school, and only 28% often recommend an apprenticeship, according to a report released earlier this year by the Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades.

“We need to change the perception and get the guidance counselors to start talking about the opportunities,” Culler said.

Even after convincing someone that a skilled trades career might be right for them, the industry still has to get them through the training process and into a job.

The Alliance’s September report found that among every 100 who start an apprenticeship, just 48 complete the program, and only 29 enter a skilled trade occupation within five years of leaving it. The numbers are similarly challenging for related postsecondary programs: Of every 100 entrants, 48 complete their programs and just 34 go on to work in a skilled trade.

Flynn described the problem as “pipeline leakiness,” which can often come down to a lack of support for workers navigating training programs. That includes seemingly basic but consequential barriers like transportation and childcare.

“We really need to be working on this together,” she said.

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.

Colette Kress, Nvidia $NVDA's interim CEO, kicked off Wednesday's gathering, the first full-staff session since Jensen Huang stepped down, by telling employees, "let's move forward," according to CNBC. The meeting took roughly 60 minutes, with employees attending in person or watching a Microsoft $MSFT Teams stream.

Nvidia made clear at the meeting that Jensen Huang, the company's co-founder, will not return as CEO, according to Bloomberg. Kress walked through the prior day's financial results and described the period as a "great quarter," according to CNBC. Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion on Tuesday, up 103% from a year earlier. Nvidia stock was down 2% on Wednesday.

Employee sentiment at the meeting was divided, according to CNBC. One attendee described the general mood as a desire for Jensen Huang's return, while another person said employees welcomed the remarks and the view into company leadership. Some current and former staff, along with Silicon Valley allies of Jensen Huang, are pushing for him to come back, according to Bloomberg.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO and left the board on Nov. 12 after reports of affairs with at least two women. U.S. officials suspect one of them, Alice Huang, of relaying information to China's intelligence services. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related. The board is searching for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates. Kress keeps her CFO role while serving as interim CEO.

#5335. Booking Holdings’ travel startup Vayo starts booking trips with AI agents, even on rival Expedia

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am

Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup launched by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel plans — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of users in its invite-only beta.

That includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group. Vayo confirmed that its AI agents book there by navigating Expedia’s website, without a direct integration or partnership for those bookings.

The company says Vayo recommends the best option for the traveler, wherever that option is booked, not just through its parent company’s brands.

Vayo is led by Mike Fridgen, a longtime Seattle entrepreneur with deep roots in travel. Booking Holdings, the parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, said last month that it plans to invest $100 million in Vayo, depending on its progress and market conditions.

Companies are still working out how to handle AI agents that use their sites on behalf of customers. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent didn’t identify itself.

When Vayo launched last month, Fridgen said it was relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, in part to avoid the risk of being blocked. Vayo says no site has blocked its bookings so far.

How the bookings work: Vayo’s new booking features work in two ways. It can book hotels, rental cars and activities through a direct connection with sister company Booking.com, and it has similar links to OpenTable for restaurants and SeatGeek for event tickets.

For flights and other bookings, its AI agents navigate the booking websites, signing in to the traveler’s existing accounts where needed and completing the purchase. Every booking requires the traveler’s approval, the company says.

If a site doesn’t allow AI agents, Vayo leaves that booking to the traveler.

Vayo uses 1Password to sign in to travelers’ accounts and, on sites other than Booking.com, Stripe’s Link agent wallet to pay, without seeing their passwords or card details, the company says. It reports a reservation as confirmed only after the supplier confirms it.

Payments and pricing: Travelers pay whichever company they book with, and Vayo is not the merchant of record. The company declined to share details on commissions, saying its partner arrangements are still taking shape and won’t factor into its recommendations.

When Booking.com has the best option, Vayo users get Genius Level 3 pricing, Booking.com’s top loyalty tier, with discounts of up to 20% on select stays.

The service is free to use during the invite-only beta. Responding to GeekWire’s questions, Vayo didn’t say how many people are using it or how many have completed a booking.

Who’s behind Vayo: Fridgen, the Vayo co-founder and CEO, was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at airfare-prediction startup Farecast, before leading Decide.com and Madrona Venture Labs.

His co-founder and CTO is Allen Chen, the former CTO of Fanatics Collectibles, who previously co-founded Seattle software startups CloudPress and DataBlade. Ian Fliflet, OfferUp’s former chief growth officer, is head of growth. Vayo had about 20 employees, all working in downtown Seattle, when it launched last month.

Next on its product roadmap, the company says it plans to work inside the messaging apps people already use, and to let groups of travelers plan trips together.

#5334. Chipotle, Macy’s, and Ally CEOs on why loyalty perks matter more as shoppers balk at high prices

When Chipotle overhauled its rewards program in April, it made perks like free chips and guac easier to snag and added half-off entrées, as diners started to balk at high prices.

For the burrito chain, the program helps it weather inflation and keep customers in the Chipotle habit. It now counts more than 24 million active members, and they drove a third of sales in the third quarter, the highest share Chipotle has reported.

“I think in this modern world, you have to be really up to speed on what’s going on with your loyalty consumer because arguably it’s the most valuable consumer within your ecosystem,” Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, on a panel moderated by this reporter.

Loyalty programs have become a front line in the fight for market share. The freebies get people in the door, but the bigger prize is the data: a detailed record of what customers buy and when, which lets brands tailor offers and makes it harder for shoppers to stray. Boatwright, Macy’s CEO Tony Spring, and Ally Financial CEO Michael Rhodes run very different businesses: Macy’s is No. 192 on the 2026 Fortune 500, Ally is No. 275, and Chipotle is No. 351. All three are leaning on that math.

Boatwright said the pull to trim perks is real. As a rewards database grows and inflation squeezes margins, he said, “The gravity pulls brands toward, ‘ How do I capture some margin here.” His own team brought him ideas for cutting rewards.

“We are unwilling as a brand to do that,” he said. “I said, come back to me with 10 ideas on how to increase value for the consumer and let’s have a conversation.”

That stance tracks with Chipotle’s refusal to chase traffic with deep discounts. In February, Boatwright said he didn’t want to “devalue our core offering” with McDonald’s-style deals and planned price increases below the rate of inflation. Loyalty perks let the chain hand its most frequent diners more value without cutting menu prices for everyone.

The same logic shaped Chipotle’s answer to GLP-1 weight-loss drugs: a high-protein menu with low-priced add-ons rather than markdowns. “You’ve got to have innovation that doesn’t discount the core offering, but meets a consumer need state,” Boatwright said.

Spring, who took over as CEO of Macy’s Inc. in February 2024, has been steering the 168-year-old department store operator’s turnaround. He said a loyalty program only works if shoppers believe it does.

“Loyalty is integral, I think, to the relationships people have with brands,” Spring said. “And we are constantly striving at Macy’s, Bloomingdale’s, and Bluemercury to make sure that the loyalty program has value in the eyes of the consumer, not in our eyes.”

The payoff comes when a shopper decides where to look first, at the mall or online. “If the Macy’s app or the Bloomingdale’s app is there and I already have rewards in my wallet, it’s going to encourage me to go there maybe and complete my activity,” he said.

Macy’s program is built to be easy to join, Spring said, with rewards that don’t depend on how a customer pays and bigger ones for Macy’s credit card holders. The most committed shoppers can earn perks like free merchandise, free delivery, and after-hours shopping. “If you are more committed to us, we want to provide that value to you,” he said.

Spring is also thinking about what happens to those perks when an AI agent does the shopping. Macy’s has started working with Google’s Gemini on agentic commerce, he said, and the priority is making sure reward points, gift cards, and delivery promises still work when a bot places the order.

Food, clothes, and home goods offer sensory experiences that financial services can’t match, and few people feel much affection for their bank. Ally Financial, which bills itself as the largest all-digital bank in the U.S., is trying anyway. In May, it rolled out Loyally, a fee-free rewards program open to customers regardless of their account balance.

“The question really is how can we add some real value for customers that gives them reasons they want to keep on coming back to our site and engaging with us,” Rhodes said. “We’ve literally had it for like six months now, but the early results are really encouraging.”

Ally is starting from a strong base, by Rhodes’ account. He said customer retention runs well over 90%, about 15% of new account volume comes through referrals, and 70% of customers are Gen Z or millennials.

Rhodes argued that AI search is raising the stakes on every customer interaction, because what customers and employees say about a brand feeds the engines that make recommendations. “There are people who spend 10 times what we spend,” he said of Ally’s marketing budget. “Yet in the AI search engines and unbranded inquiries in consumer banking, we show up number one.”

The harder balance is rewarding regulars while still persuading new customers to try a brand. Spring said that’s where a retailer’s customer data comes in: breaking shoppers into cohorts and targeting each one, both to drive new traffic and to “create extraordinary value for your highest, most loyal consumers.”

“It’s not a one-size-fits-all approach,” Spring said. “It needs to be very bespoke. And you have to leverage tools like, dare I say, AI.”

Boatwright said every change to Chipotle’s program aims to draw more users in at the top of the funnel, then “make it much more sticky within the funnel and get those consumers coming back more often.”

The next test may come when the customer isn’t the one searching. Boatwright said agentic AI ordering is coming whether brands are ready or not, and Chipotle has to make sure it shows up “when you ask your agent, tell me the best burrito in town.”

Phil Wahba is a senior writer at Fortune primarily focused on leadership coverage, with a prior focus on retail.

#5333. 12 Speaker of the House firsts, from Frederick Muhlenberg to Kevin McCarthy

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These Speaker of the House firsts, from Frederick Muhlenberg in 1789 to Kevin McCarthy's 2023 removal, trace how the office gained, lost and reshaped its power

The U.S. Constitution names only one officer of the House of Representatives. Article I says the House shall choose its Speaker and other officers. It says nothing more about the job. Everything else that defines the speakership has been settled by the House itself since 1789. That includes how much power the office carries, how a member wins it and how a Speaker can lose it.

As a result, the office's history reads as a record of improvisation. Practices that look fixed today often began as a single Speaker's ruling, a floor fight or an election result without precedent. Many of these firsts mark a moment when the balance of power inside the chamber shifted. Sometimes it moved toward the Speaker, and sometimes away.

The Speaker presides over the House and controls much of its agenda, including which bills reach the floor and when. The office also stands second in the presidential line of succession, behind the vice president. That placement comes from the Presidential Succession Act of 1947.

This timeline gathers 12 Speaker of the House firsts in chronological order. It is a selection, not a complete record of every precedent the office has set. It begins in April 1789, when the 1st Congress reached a quorum and elected Frederick Muhlenberg of Pennsylvania. It ends in October 2023, when the House removed a sitting Speaker through a motion to vacate for the first time.

In between are the entries that trace the job's reach. One Speaker won the post on his first day as a member. Another later moved to the White House. One changed what counts as a quorum. A later Speaker saw his powers cut by insurgents in his own party working with the opposition. The list also covers the longest total tenure and the longest unbroken run. It includes a party's return to the majority after decades in the minority. It also marks the first woman to hold the gavel and her return to the post years later.

Each entry stands on its own. Readers can start with the founding-era Speakers or jump to the 2023 fight over the gavel, which took 15 ballots to settle. The entries show how the House has expanded, limited and contested the Speaker's authority over time.

Frederick Muhlenberg, a Pennsylvania representative, became the first Speaker of the House in April 1789. Members chose him once the chamber gathered a quorum during the 1st Congress.

The new Congress was due to open in March 1789 in New York, then the seat of the federal government. Too few representatives had arrived to conduct business. The House could not organize itself or elect officers until enough members reached the city. Once a quorum assembled in April, choosing a presiding officer was among its first acts.

Muhlenberg brought prior experience in running a legislature to the post. He had served in the Continental Congress and had presided over the Pennsylvania Assembly. He was also president of the Pennsylvania convention that ratified the Constitution in 1787.

Muhlenberg was born in 1750 in Trappe, Pennsylvania. He was ordained as a Lutheran minister before turning to public office. His father, Henry Melchior Muhlenberg, organized the first Lutheran synod in North America. His brother Peter Muhlenberg served as a general in the Continental Army.

Henry Clay, a Kentucky representative, was elected Speaker of the House in 1811 on his first day as a House member. He held the post in three separate stretches, the last ending in 1825.

The vote came on Nov. 4, 1811, when the 12th Congress convened. Clay was not new to national politics. He had already served two short stints in the U.S. Senate, filling unexpired terms. The House was a different setting. Members chose a newcomer to lead them before he had cast a single vote in the chamber.

Clay arrived as a leader of the War Hawks. This group of mostly Southern and Western members pressed for a harder line against Britain. As Speaker, he used his authority to advance that agenda. Congress declared war on Britain in June 1812, starting the War of 1812.

Thomas Brackett Reed, a Maine Republican, was Speaker of the House from 1889 to 1891. In January 1890, he ruled that members sitting in the chamber but not voting would count toward a quorum. The ruling ended the minority's ability to stall the House by staying silent.

The tactic Reed confronted was known as the "disappearing quorum." The Constitution requires a majority of the House to be present to do business. Minority members could attend a session and simply decline to answer the roll call. They were then recorded as absent.

If enough of them stayed quiet, the count fell short of a majority. The House could not act, even with most of its members physically in the room. When the majority party held a narrow edge, a determined minority could freeze the legislative calendar this way.

Sam Rayburn, a Texas Democrat, holds the record for the most total time as Speaker of the House. Across three separate stretches between 1940 and 1961, he held the gavel for about 17 years. No one else has served longer in the office.

His first stretch began in September 1940. Rayburn, then the House majority leader, was elected Speaker after the death of Speaker William Bankhead of Alabama. He kept the post until 1947.

The breaks in his tenure came from elections, not from any challenge inside his own party. Republicans won control of the House for two Congresses during his career. The first ran from 1947 to 1949, and the second from 1953 to 1955. Each time, Rayburn led House Democrats as minority leader.

His second stretch as Speaker ran from 1949 to 1953. His third began in 1955 and lasted until his death from cancer in November 1961. He was still Speaker when he died.

Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, became Speaker of the House in January 1995. His party had won control of the chamber in the 1994 midterm elections, ending a run of Democratic majorities that dated to the 1950s.

Across those decades, every Speaker was a Democrat. Democrats also chaired every standing committee and set the floor schedule.

Gingrich first won his seat in 1978 and took office in January 1979. Through the 1980s, he built a reputation as a combative critic of the Democratic leadership. House Republicans elected him minority whip in 1989, making him the party's second-ranking leader in the chamber.

In September 1994, House Republicans unveiled the Contract with America, a campaign platform Gingrich helped shape. More than 300 Republican House candidates signed it. The document promised votes on 10 bills within the first 100 days of a Republican-led Congress. Its proposals included a balanced budget amendment, a line-item veto and changes to welfare.

Nancy Pelosi was elected Speaker of the House again on Jan. 3, 2019. The vote made her the first former Speaker to win back the gavel after a break since Sam Rayburn did so in 1955.

Her return came eight years after she lost the post. Pelosi first held the speakership from 2007 until January 2011. Republicans won control of the House in the 2010 midterm elections, and she became minority leader.

Two Republicans held the gavel during her years out of the office. John Boehner of Ohio served as Speaker from 2011 until he resigned in 2015. Paul Ryan of Wisconsin followed him and served until the end of the 115th Congress in January 2019.

Democrats regained a House majority in the 2018 midterm elections. That result set up Pelosi's second election as Speaker on the opening day of the 116th Congress.

Kevin McCarthy became the first Speaker of the House removed from office by a vote of the full chamber. On Oct. 3, 2023, the House ousted the California Republican through a motion to vacate the chair. He had held the gavel for less than nine months.

A motion to vacate is a resolution that declares the Speaker's office empty. If a majority of members voting approves it, the Speaker loses the post immediately.

Rep. Matt Gaetz, a Florida Republican, filed the motion on Oct. 2, 2023. It came two days after the House, under McCarthy, passed a stopgap spending bill with Democratic votes. That measure kept the federal government open and averted a shutdown.

The path to the vote ran through the rules McCarthy accepted to win the speakership that January. Those rules let any single House member force a vote on removing the Speaker. Under the previous Congress, a motion to vacate needed the backing of a party caucus or conference.

The 1st Congress had a heavy agenda. It created the departments of State, War and the Treasury. It set up the federal court system through the Judiciary Act of 1789. It also approved 12 proposed constitutional amendments. As Speaker, Muhlenberg signed the enrolled resolution that sent them to the states in 1789. Vice President John Adams signed it as well, as president of the Senate. The states ratified 10 of the amendments, which became the Bill of Rights.

Muhlenberg did not hold the gavel in the 2nd Congress, which met from 1791 to 1793. Jonathan Trumbull Jr. of Connecticut served as Speaker instead. Muhlenberg then returned to the chair, serving a second stretch from 1793 to 1795. That return made him the first person to hold the speakership on two nonconsecutive occasions.

The early speakership was mainly a presiding role. The Speaker kept order, recognized members during debate and ruled on procedure. Muhlenberg stayed in the House until 1797. He died in 1801 in Lancaster, Pennsylvania.

His main tool was committee assignments. House rules at the time let the Speaker appoint committee members. Clay placed allies on the committees that handled foreign affairs and military matters. That gave the Speaker a direct hand in shaping which bills moved and how.

Clay's approach turned the speakership into a center of political power. Earlier Speakers had acted mostly as presiding officers. Clay used the chair to steer legislation and policy as well as to run debate.

His first stretch ended in January 1814. He resigned the speakership to join the U.S. delegation that negotiated peace with Britain. That delegation produced the Treaty of Ghent, signed in December 1814.

Clay returned to the House and was elected Speaker again in 1815. During his second stretch, Congress took up the dispute over Missouri's admission as a state. Clay played a central role in the Missouri Compromise of 1820. He left the chair later that year.

His third stretch began in 1823. It ended in 1825, when Clay left the House to become secretary of state under President John Quincy Adams. He later returned to the Senate and ran for president three times without winning.

James K. Polk is the only Speaker of the House who went on to become president. The Tennessee Democrat held the gavel from 1835 to 1839, then served in the White House from 1845 to 1849.

Polk was born in North Carolina in 1795 and built his political career in Tennessee. He entered the House in 1825. He was a close ally of Andrew Jackson. Supporters called him "Young Hickory," a nod to Jackson's nickname, "Old Hickory."

His speakership covered the 24th and 25th Congresses. Polk won the post in 1835 by defeating John Bell, a fellow Tennessean. The chamber he led was split between Jacksonian Democrats and the new Whig Party, which had formed in opposition to Jackson.

Those divisions made the job contentious. Whig members challenged his rulings and pressed him on procedure. In 1836 the House also adopted the "gag rule," which tabled antislavery petitions without debate. Fights over that rule ran through his time in the chair.

Polk left the House in 1839 to become governor of Tennessee. He then lost races for that office in 1841 and 1843. Those defeats left him without a public post as the 1844 presidential contest approached.

The Democratic National Convention met in Baltimore in 1844. Martin Van Buren arrived as the front-runner but could not secure the nomination. Delegates turned to Polk, a compromise candidate, on the ninth ballot.

In the general election, Polk defeated the Whig nominee, Henry Clay. He pledged to serve a single term and kept that promise.

His presidency expanded U.S. territory. The 1846 Oregon Treaty with Britain set the northwestern boundary at the 49th parallel. The Mexican-American War ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848. That treaty brought California and much of the Southwest under U.S. control.

At home, Polk restored the Independent Treasury system. He also signed the Walker Tariff, which lowered import duties.

Polk left office in March 1849. His successor was Zachary Taylor, a Whig. Polk died of cholera in Nashville that June.

Reed stopped relying on roll-call responses alone. He directed the clerk to record the names of members who were present but refusing to vote. Those members were then counted toward the quorum. Democrats protested loudly from the floor, but the ruling stood.

The House then wrote the principle into its rules for that Congress. The package became known as the Reed Rules. It also gave the Speaker more room to rule out motions offered only to delay business.

The new method was tested in court. In United States v. Ballin, decided in 1892, the Supreme Court upheld the House's power to set its own way of determining whether a quorum was present.

The episode is tied to Reed's nickname, "Czar Reed." Critics used the label to describe the control he exercised over the floor. The ruling shifted power away from the minority and toward the Speaker and the majority party.

Democrats dropped the counting rule after they took control of the House following Reed's first speakership. They adopted their own version of it in 1894. Reed later returned to the chair, serving as Speaker again from 1895 to 1899.

In March 1910, a coalition of insurgent Republicans and Democrats removed Speaker Joseph G. Cannon from the House Rules Committee. The vote broke the Speaker's control over which bills reached the floor and how they were debated.

Cannon, an Illinois Republican, held the speakership from 1903 to 1911. Colleagues and the press knew him as "Uncle Joe." In that era, the Speaker appointed members to House committees and also chaired the Rules Committee.

Those two powers worked together. Committee assignments let Cannon reward allies and sideline critics. Control of the Rules Committee let him decide when legislation came up for a vote and under what terms.

Cannon used that leverage to slow measures he opposed, including proposals backed by progressive members of his own party. Republicans from the Midwest and West who wanted reform found their bills stalled. They became known as insurgents.

The decisive challenge came from George Norris, a Republican representative from Nebraska. He introduced a resolution to change how the Rules Committee was chosen. Cannon's supporters argued that the resolution was out of order. The dispute carried through several days of floor debate.

Norris's measure passed when Democrats joined the insurgents. It expanded the Rules Committee, gave the full House the power to elect the committee's members and barred the Speaker from sitting on it.

Cannon answered the defeat by inviting a motion to declare the chair vacant. Albert Burleson, a Texas Democrat, offered it. The motion failed. Many insurgents who had voted to curb Cannon's powers would not vote to remove him from office.

Cannon remained Speaker until the end of that Congress. Democrats then won control of the House in the 1910 midterm elections. Missouri Democrat Champ Clark became Speaker in 1911. The new majority also moved committee assignment power away from the Speaker.

The Speaker has not served on the Rules Committee since the 1910 vote. Later Speakers shaped the panel through their party's leadership rather than by holding a seat on it.

Cannon's name remains on Capitol Hill. The Cannon House Office Building, completed in 1908, is the oldest of the House office buildings.

That span put him in the chair under four presidents: Franklin D. Roosevelt, Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John F. Kennedy. Eisenhower was a Republican. Rayburn spent much of the late 1950s as a Democratic Speaker working with a president from the other party.

Rayburn worked through personal relationships with members. He hosted lawmakers in a private room in the Capitol known as the "Board of Education," where they gathered after hours. Truman, then vice president, was in that room on April 12, 1945. There he received a call summoning him to the White House. At the White House, he learned that Roosevelt had died.

Rayburn also served as a mentor to Lyndon B. Johnson, a fellow Texan. Johnson began his House career in the 1930s before moving on to the Senate.

Rayburn first entered the House in 1913. He represented a district in northeast Texas that included his hometown of Bonham. Before Congress, he had served as speaker of the Texas House of Representatives.

John McCormack of Massachusetts succeeded him as Speaker in January 1962. The Rayburn House Office Building, which houses congressional offices on Capitol Hill, carries his name.

Thomas P. "Tip" O'Neill, a Massachusetts Democrat, served as Speaker of the House from 1977 to 1987. His 10 years in the chair are the longest continuous tenure in the office's history.

O'Neill took the gavel in January 1977, at the opening of the 95th Congress. He succeeded Carl Albert of Oklahoma, who had retired. O'Neill had already moved up through the Democratic leadership. He served as majority whip and then as majority leader under Albert.

O'Neill was born in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1912. Before reaching Congress, he served in the Massachusetts House of Representatives and rose to become its speaker. He then won the U.S. House seat that John F. Kennedy gave up to run for the Senate. O'Neill took that seat in 1953.

His speakership spanned five consecutive Congresses, the 95th through the 99th. Sam Rayburn of Texas holds the record for total time as Speaker. Rayburn's service, though, was broken into separate stretches by periods of Republican control. O'Neill held the gavel without interruption from his first election as Speaker until his departure.

O'Neill's decade as Speaker overlapped two presidents. His first four years came under Jimmy Carter, a fellow Democrat. The remaining six came under Ronald Reagan, a Republican. Reagan drew on votes from conservative Democrats to pass his 1981 tax and budget plans over O'Neill's opposition.

The two men also reached agreements. In 1983, O'Neill and Reagan backed a bipartisan package of Social Security changes. The package built on recommendations from a commission chaired by Alan Greenspan.

Live television coverage of the House began during his speakership. C-SPAN started carrying House floor proceedings in March 1979, early in the 96th Congress.

O'Neill did not run for reelection in 1986. He left Congress when his term ended in January 1987. Jim Wright of Texas, the majority leader, succeeded him as Speaker. O'Neill died in Boston in January 1994.

His memoir, Man of the House, written with William Novak, came out in 1987. The phrase "All politics is local" became the saying most closely associated with him. It also became the title of a book he wrote with Gary Hymel, published in 1994.

The 1994 losses extended to the Democratic leadership. Speaker Tom Foley, a Democrat from Washington state, lost his own seat. He was the first sitting Speaker defeated for reelection since 1862.

Once in charge, the new majority rewrote House rules. Committee chairs became subject to a limit of three consecutive terms. The Speaker's own tenure was capped at four consecutive terms. The House also abolished three committees and cut committee staff by about a third. The eliminated panels were the District of Columbia, Merchant Marine and Fisheries, and Post Office and Civil Service committees.

Gingrich's speakership also brought clashes with President Bill Clinton over the federal budget. Two government shutdowns followed. The first lasted from Nov. 14 to Nov. 19, 1995. The longer one ran from Dec. 16, 1995, to Jan. 6, 1996.

In January 1997, the House reprimanded Gingrich over an ethics case and assessed him a $300,000 penalty. After Republicans lost House seats in the 1998 midterms, he announced he would step down as Speaker. He left Congress in January 1999.

Nancy Pelosi became the first woman to serve as Speaker of the House on Jan. 4, 2007. The California Democrat won the post on the opening day of the 110th Congress, more than two centuries after the first Speaker took the chair in 1789.

Her election followed the 2006 midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of the House. Pelosi took the gavel from Dennis Hastert, an Illinois Republican who had held it since 1999.

Pelosi reached the speakership by rising through her party's House leadership. Her Democratic colleagues elected her whip in 2001. She became the party's top leader in the House in January 2003. That made her the first woman to lead a major party in either chamber of Congress.

Her congressional career began in San Francisco. She won her House seat in a 1987 special election and represented a San Francisco district for decades afterward. She also became the first Italian American to serve as Speaker.

Her roots are in Baltimore, where she was born. Her father, Thomas D'Alesandro Jr., represented a Maryland district in the House and later served as mayor of Baltimore.

The 2007 vote also changed the presidential line of succession. No woman had ever stood as high in that line as Pelosi did once she took the gavel.

The milestone closed a long gap for women in the House. Jeannette Rankin, a Montana Republican, became the first woman elected to Congress in 1916. She took her seat the following year. Women served in the House for about nine decades before one held its top post.

Pelosi's first stretch as Speaker covered four years and two Congresses. During that time, the House passed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, which President Barack Obama signed in February 2009. The House also passed the Affordable Care Act, and Obama signed the health care law in March 2010.

That stretch ended after the 2010 midterm elections, when Republicans won back the House majority. John Boehner, an Ohio Republican, succeeded her as Speaker in January 2011.

Her return required support from critics inside her own party. A group of House Democrats pushed for new leadership after the midterms. Pelosi won over enough of them in part by agreeing to limit how long she would serve as Speaker. Several Democrats still voted for other candidates when the full House chose its Speaker.

The gap between the two comebacks spans more than six decades. Rayburn regained the office in 1955 after Republicans controlled the House for two years. Pelosi's absence lasted four times as long as his.

Pelosi held the gavel for two more Congresses, the 116th and the 117th. During that stretch she presided over the House as it impeached President Donald Trump twice. The first impeachment came in December 2019 and the second in January 2021. After the 2020 elections, she led a narrow Democratic majority.

Republicans won the House in the 2022 midterm elections. Pelosi then announced she would not seek a leadership post in the next Congress. Hakeem Jeffries of New York succeeded her as leader of House Democrats.

Her second stretch as Speaker ended in January 2023. Across her two stints, she spent eight years in the office.

Kevin McCarthy, a California Republican, became Speaker of the House in the early hours of Jan. 7, 2023, on the 15th ballot. He reached the gavel only after 14 earlier rounds of voting failed to produce a winner.

The contest opened on Jan. 3, 2023, the first day of the 118th Congress. Electing a Speaker is the first order of business in a new House. Until that vote is settled, members-elect cannot take the oath of office. The chamber also cannot adopt its rules, form committees or pass legislation.

Republicans had won a narrow House majority in the 2022 midterm elections. McCarthy had led the House Republican conference since 2019, and he was the party's nominee for Speaker. To win, a candidate needs a majority of the members who vote for a named person. With so few seats to spare, a small bloc of Republicans could keep him below that line.

That bloc formed on the opening day. A group of conservative Republicans withheld their support and cast votes for other names instead. Democrats backed their own leader, Hakeem Jeffries of New York, on every ballot. Neither candidate could reach a majority, and the House kept voting.

The standoff stretched across several days of roll calls. McCarthy and his allies negotiated with the holdouts between votes. Several of those members moved into his column on Jan. 6. The rest did not switch outright.

On the 15th ballot, the final holdouts voted present rather than naming another candidate. A present vote does not count toward the total of members voting for a named person. That lowered the number McCarthy needed, and he cleared it shortly after midnight.

Rep. Hal Rogers of Kentucky, the dean of the House, administered the Speaker's oath to McCarthy. McCarthy then swore in the other members-elect as a group. With that step done, the House could adopt its rules and begin its formal work for the new Congress.

An earlier attempt to remove a Speaker this way never reached the floor. In 2015, Rep. Mark Meadows of North Carolina filed a motion to vacate against Speaker John Boehner. The House never voted on it. Boehner announced his resignation later that year.

McCarthy's removal left the chamber without an elected Speaker. Patrick McHenry, a North Carolina Republican, stepped in as Speaker pro tempore. His name sat at the top of a confidential list of successors McCarthy had filed with the House Clerk. A House rule adopted after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks requires each new Speaker to submit such a list.

House Republicans put forward several nominees for the job over the following weeks. The search ended on Oct. 25, 2023, when the House elected Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, as Speaker.

McCarthy did not run to reclaim the post. He left Congress at the end of 2023.

#5332. Your Best Employees May Be the Ones Nobody Hears From

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The people who speak most confidently in meetings aren’t always the people with the best ideas. Here’s how leaders can stop overlooking valuable talent.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every workplace has someone who seems to have an answer for everything. They’re quick to contribute in meetings, comfortable challenging colleagues and rarely hesitate when an executive asks for an opinion.

Then there’s the employee who listens carefully, takes notes and says very little.

Which one gets noticed? Too often, it’s the person who speaks first.

I’ve led and worked with teams across consulting, technology and marketing, and I’ve learned to be careful about equating confidence with capability. People communicate differently. Some think through problems by talking. Others need time to consider the information before forming an opinion.

Neither approach automatically produces better judgment. But many workplaces reward one more visibly than the other.

Think about how most brainstorming sessions operate. A leader presents a problem and asks for ideas. Someone immediately offers a suggestion. Another person agrees, adds something, and the conversation moves forward.

Within minutes, a direction begins to emerge. The session appears productive. People are engaged, ideas are flowing, and decisions are being made.

If the first confident suggestion becomes the foundation for the discussion, everyone else may spend the meeting reacting to that idea instead of considering alternatives.

This is especially problematic when the most senior person speaks first. Employees may hesitate to challenge an executive, even when they recognize a weakness in the proposed approach.

That’s why I prefer giving people the problem to think about before asking them to solve it together. Even a short explanation sent ahead of a meeting can change the conversation. People arrive with their own observations rather than immediately responding to whoever speaks first.

Some employees contribute best through discussion. Others communicate more effectively in writing or smaller groups. A leader who relies exclusively on group meetings may never hear valuable insights from people who dislike competing for attention.

I would build more than one opportunity for participation into important decisions. Ask employees to submit their observations before a meeting. Invite questions afterward. Create smaller working groups when a topic requires deeper thinking.

And when someone who rarely speaks contributes an idea, give it the same consideration you would give a suggestion from your most outspoken colleague.

The objective isn’t to force quiet employees to become more extroverted. It’s to make sure communication style doesn’t determine whose judgment matters.

A leader can repeatedly tell employees that every idea is welcome. Those words mean very little if people watch a colleague get embarrassed for disagreeing.

Employees notice how leaders respond to criticism, particularly when the criticism is valid. In my earlier Entrepreneur article about transparent decision-making, I discussed why explaining how decisions are made is essential to building organizational trust.

That principle extends to brainstorming. You don’t need to accept every suggestion. But people should understand why an idea was adopted, rejected or deferred.

If you ask for different perspectives and then consistently reward agreement, employees will eventually stop offering them.

There is another dimension to this problem. Even when quiet employees perform exceptionally well, their contributions can remain invisible beyond their immediate managers.

They receive positive feedback, but the opportunities that lead to career advancement go elsewhere. I previously explored this distinction between receiving advice and gaining access to opportunity, and it raises a useful question for business owners: Are you developing capable employees, or are you also making sure their capabilities are recognized?

When someone does excellent work, bring that contribution into conversations where decisions about responsibility, promotions and opportunities are being made. Don’t reserve high-visibility assignments for the people who are already comfortable promoting themselves.

Here’s something I would encourage every founder to try.

Think about your last five important team decisions. Who contributed most of the ideas? Whose recommendations shaped the final outcome? Were the same three or four people consistently heard?

Now look at who wasn’t part of those conversations. Were they excluded because they lacked relevant expertise, or because nobody created an opportunity for them to contribute?

You may find that the organization has more insight available than its meetings suggest.

Try rotating who leads discussions. Ask people to share independent recommendations before opening the floor. Review whether important assignments are distributed according to capability or visibility.

These changes don’t require a new leadership program or expensive technology. They require awareness of how influence operates inside your business.

I’m not suggesting that confident employees should speak less or that every idea deserves equal weight. Organizations need people who can articulate their thinking, make decisions and move work forward.

But confidence should never become a substitute for sound reasoning. The strongest leaders create conditions in which employees can question assumptions without worrying about how that will affect their standing. They also recognize that sometimes the person who speaks last has been thinking about the problem longer than anyone else.

Before your next brainstorming session, consider whether you’re hearing from the people with the most to contribute or simply the people most comfortable contributing.

Your best idea may already be sitting in the room. You might just need to make space for it.

Every workplace has someone who seems to have an answer for everything. They’re quick to contribute in meetings, comfortable challenging colleagues and rarely hesitate when an executive asks for an opinion.

Then there’s the employee who listens carefully, takes notes and says very little.

Which one gets noticed? Too often, it’s the person who speaks first.

#5331. Seattle fleet tracking company Zonar names Atlanta-based CEO, who says HQ is staying put

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a new CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no plans to change that.” He said he visits the company’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

Consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based company acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software company Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and says it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli said Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

Zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the company.

Zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but said Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by new pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

Zonar has added 1,000 new customers so far this year, a spokesperson said. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the company’s 2026 plan, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli said.

Zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli said Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He said those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the big players.”

Consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

“Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli said. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”

Founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The company cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

Hiring elite engineers or proven revenue leaders in 2026?

Great teams still win, and finding them is harder than ever. That’s why GeekWire teamed up with Prime Team Partners on GeekWork, a hiring initiative built to help companies connect with exceptional talent.

#5330. Oklahoma’s governor sees universities as ‘stuck in their ways.’ His fix, a 3-year bachelor’s degree, is already spreading fast

Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt has a problem with the four-year degree, and he brought it to a room full of the people who hire its graduates.

“The academic community are kind of stuck in their ways. They don’t like to change,” Stitt said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, on a panel with U.S. Steel CEO David Burritt. He said when he digs into the degree programs at the University of Oklahoma and Oklahoma State, “there’s a book this thick and then you’ve got like three people graduating from these different things.”

He added: “I’m not saying that degree is not important, but you can’t be all things [to] all people.”

His fix is a 90-credit bachelor’s degree, 30 credits short of the standard 120, or roughly a year less of tuition. In-state tuition and fees at public four-year colleges averaged $11,950 in the 2024-25 school year, according to the College Board. Stitt said the idea is to keep the rigor of the requirements, trim some electives, and “get kids ready for the workforce quicker.”

RAND counted 119 reduced-credit bachelor’s programs publicly announced across the U.S. as of May 2026, most of them in “applied and workforce-facing fields.” Only five were announced in 2024. In 2026 alone, RAND counted 50 through May, when its data collection ended, and Jason Lee, a senior policy researcher at RAND and the report’s lead author, told Fortune he has seen roughly 100 more announcements since. That puts this year at about 150, though Lee said the newer count hasn’t been through RAND’s quality-assurance review and should be treated as approximate.

Stitt signed an executive order in February ordering a 90-day study of 90-credit “accelerated” degrees, and the Legislature followed with HB 3315, which required the State Regents to study feasibility. In June, the regents took action to create a framework for the degrees.

“A three-year degree speeds up workforce entry and makes so much sense for students who are ready to work and support a family, right here in Oklahoma,” Stitt said in a statement at the time.

On Sept. 3, the regents approved four reduced-credit degrees ranging from 90 to 103 credit hours, according to the Oklahoma Council of Public Affairs: social work at the University of Oklahoma, two at Oklahoma State, in artificial intelligence and in business, and workforce development at Rogers State University.

“A college degree doesn’t have to take four years just because it always has,” Stitt posted on X.

The University of Oklahoma told Fortune that it sees itself “at the forefront of rethinking traditional approaches to higher education to better serve students and meet Oklahoma’s workforce needs,” leading the way in developing three-year bachelor’s degrees, while ensuring traditional degree programs are structured to avoid unnecessary credit hours that can delay graduation.

Other states are moving, too. Tennessee’s higher education commission approved a policy in July allowing bachelor’s degrees of as few as 90 credit hours. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott directed the state’s coordinating board to develop pathways in August. The University of North Carolina system approved a pilot in April, and 11 campuses have submitted proposals, according to the James G. Martin Center.

Through May, most of the growth came from individual colleges, especially private ones, Lee told Fortune, though states and accreditors shaped it too, since both have a hand in approving new programs. Since then, he said, “it seems to have become much more common for state actors to encourage these programs at their public universities,” as in Oklahoma, Tennessee, and Texas. Ohio and Indiana have gone further, he said, and required their public universities to adopt them.

The three-year degree tests an old question in economics: how much of a degree’s value comes from what students learn, and how much from what it tells employers. Michael Spence shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in economics, in part, for showing how education can work as a signal, costly proof of ability that employers can’t see directly. A shorter degree is cheaper to get. Nobody knows yet whether it signals as much. Much of Europe has run three-year bachelor’s degrees since the Bologna reforms began in 1999.

RAND found that business, information technology, and cybersecurity look most workable for shorter degrees, while fields with clinical or licensing requirements are less adaptable. How graduate schools, employers, and licensing boards will treat the degrees remains uncertain, RAND found.

“These programs are too nascent to follow graduates into the workforce,” Lee told Fortune.

“We don’t have employers who said, ‘Gee, we’ve had three-year graduates,’” Madeleine Green, executive director of the College-in-3 Exchange, told Inside Higher Ed this month.

The programs are still small. Johnson & Wales University has 135 students across four three-year programs, and Weber State has 30 across three, according to Inside Higher Ed.

Faculty groups have pushed back. The American Association of University Professors and the American Federation of Teachers objected to Massachusetts’ approvals on grounds of “academic integrity.”

“This is not innovation. This is just cutting corners,” AAUP president Todd Wolfson told the Associated Press in August. A year less of tuition is also a year less of revenue for the schools.

Stitt’s other pitch to the CEOs was apprenticeships. He said he had visited Switzerland and Germany, where compulsory education stops after the first year of high school and students start working inside companies, and that Oklahoma made liability insurance fixes so companies could take on high school students. He told the room about a 19-year-old in Switzerland who wanted to be an architect. After three years at an architecture firm, she could work as a draftsperson, and university was still open to her.

“We’ve got to rethink that in our workforce needs here in the U.S.,” Stitt said.

[This report has been updated with comments from Rand’s Jason Lee.]

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5329. U.S. charges Russian man with stalking Palantir workers over Ukraine work

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Prosecutors say Igor D'iu was recruited over Telegram to surveil employees of a Palo Alto company because of its help to Ukraine

The Justice Department announced charges on Wednesday against Russian national Igor D'iu, accusing him of acting as an agent of Russia and stalking employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company. A federal grand jury indicted him on four counts: conspiracy to act as a foreign agent, acting as a foreign agent without notice to the Attorney General, interstate stalking and fraud in connection with identification documents.

The department did not name the company, which has an office in Palo Alto, California. The company was Palantir $PLTR Technologies, Bloomberg revealed. According to CBS News, context in the charging documents hints that the company may be Palantir. Palantir did not immediately respond to requests for comment, according to both outlets.

"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian of the Northern District of California said in a statement.

According to the indictment and a supporting affidavit, co-conspirators recruited D'iu through Telegram in 2026. They told him the work was for "the Motherland" and tasked him with collecting intelligence on the company, citing its supply of weapons used against Russia in Ukraine. He traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City in June, where he was connected with a person who helped him cross the U.S. border, prosecutors say.

The co-conspirators told him to buy laptops, phones, networking equipment and remote access software, the affidavit says. They directed him to photograph employees' laptop screens at a coffee shop near the Palo Alto office and to place a laptop near the company so they could access it remotely.

Prosecutors say D'iu searched for employees' home addresses, including that of a senior executive. On or about Sept. 3, he followed a female employee for close to 30 miles from Palo Alto toward San Francisco, running a red light to stay behind her. She called 911 and drove to a San Francisco police station, and D'iu ended the pursuit, according to the Justice Department.

Investigators intercepted two packages from overseas containing a falsified California ID card, an altered U.S. passport and a Social Security card in the name "Hugo Landry Johns," the affidavit says. FBI agents searched D'iu and his East Palo Alto residence in October. They recovered about $18,000 in cash, two laptops, two iPhones, two Russian passports and a notebook of 10 addresses, many matching employees' residences. The notebook also held profiles of at least three employees.

The FBI also uncovered exchanges in which co-conspirators shared pictures and addresses for at least four employees and instructed D'iu to pretend to be a food courier, according to CBS News.

The U.S. Attorney's Office said D'iu was arrested on Oct. 30. He first appeared in court on Nov. 2 and is still being held by federal authorities. His next appearance is scheduled for Nov. 24.

If convicted, D'iu faces up to 10 years in prison on the foreign-agent count without notice to the Attorney General, up to five years each on the conspiracy and stalking counts, and up to one year on the fraud count. An indictment alleges crimes, and defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.
