#5328. Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 8:37 am

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software company, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

His co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health company Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health plans that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their plans “after we’ve built our product.”

But after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the plan.

Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

“Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it says.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”

Kelman, by his own account, is new to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman said the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:

Chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software company he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in new blood.”

The Sojourn site says the company is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”

That fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.”

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn plans to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”

A new health plan typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the company hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a new mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He said at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”

He appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

#5327. Squeezed by rising costs, Gen Z is still buying wellness and lip gloss

Gen Z is still spending. It’s just far more deliberate about where the money goes, and beauty and wellness keep making the cut, executives from Ulta Beauty, Pacsun, and Upstart said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Tuesday.

The squeeze on young consumers is real. Upstart cofounder and CEO Paul Gu told Fortune‘s Ellie Austin that the economy looks strong on paper, with record retail sales, a solid job market, and stocks near all-time highs. The catch for people in their twenties, he said, is simple: “Stuff costs too much money.”

That pressure shows up in the data. Deloitte’s 2026 Gen Z and Millennial Survey found that 55% of Gen Z are delaying major life decisions, such as starting a family or launching a business, because of their finances.

Credit is part of the problem. “We see that something like nearly 60% of all Gen Z consumers just don’t even bother to apply for credit because they assume they’re going to be rejected,” said Gu, who took over as CEO of the AI lending company in May. “I think they’re basically right. You can’t really go to a bank without a long credit history and expect to get approved for a meaningful amount of credit when you need it… That number, by the way, is almost three times as high as what you would see for older Americans.”

For retailers, that squeeze hasn’t meant cheaper baskets. Ulta Beauty president and CEO Kecia Steelman, No. 39 on Fortune‘s 2026 Most Powerful Women list, said young shoppers aren’t choosing between feeling secure and treating themselves. “It’s a little bit of a mix of both,” she said.

“We don’t see the consumer trading down, and we don’t see this segment of the consumer demographic trading down either,” Steelman said. “Value is the perception of: Is it worth my investment in the dollars that I have?… They’re being a lot more conservative, but I just happen to be in a great category that they’re choosing. They’re prioritizing beauty and wellness.”

The numbers back her up. Ulta, a Fortune 500 company with $12.4 billion in revenue last fiscal year, raised its full-year guidance in August after second-quarter comparable sales rose 3.8%. That tracks with what Bank of America has called Gen Z’s “treat culture”: small, frequent purchases that many young people see as necessities.

Pacsun CEO Brieane Olson sees the same discipline. Young shoppers put “a lot more intentionality behind purchase than we’ve seen in the past,” she said, calling their decisions “purposeful and intentional.”

Olson pointed to Pacsun’s annual youth research, which found that wellness “ranks at the very highest in terms of what they are trying to achieve.” In the 2026 edition, conducted with GlobalData and published in September, 59% of more than 6,000 respondents aged 11 to 24 named being mentally healthy as a top goal by age 35.

Social media may spark interest, but both CEOs said purchases still tend to happen in person. Ulta has 47 million loyalty members, and 75% of its sales come from people who shop only in stores, Steelman said. Just 5% come from shoppers who buy only online. Gen Z also makes up 65% of Ulta’s store associates.

“TikTok has definitely changed the way that things can go viral in a very short period of time. But it’s not the thing that’s really driving the Gen Z consumer,” Steelman said. “I think that’s where they have the discovery. But human connection is still what makes them make the decision.”

Olson said Pacsun is seeing “a large return to in-person shopping” among 16- to 24-year-olds. The retailer also gives young customers a direct say through its youth advisory council. A 13-year-old member recently suggested an after-hours shopping event for friends, Olson said, and it grossed close to what Pacsun’s stores bring in per hour on Black Friday.

For companies that want Gen Z’s business, Gu said the starting point is to stop turning them away. Young people apply for credit and get rejected, he said. “This is like the daily experience of young consumers, and that is no way to build a relationship with them.”

Allie Garfinkle is a senior writer and editor at Fortune, where she runs Term Sheet; leads coverage of private capital, investors, and startups; and co-chairs the Brainstorm conference series.

#5326. I’ve Built and Sold Several Tech Companies. Here’s What I Know About Building a Business That People Trust

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I used to think a great product would sell itself, but building several companies taught me customers need more proof than that.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’ve been building technology companies for more than two decades.

When I started my first business at 18, selling computers in Romania, my “brand” was nonexistent. Like any entrepreneur starting out, I had to convince people to take a chance on a company they didn’t know. That’s far from easy.

In 2003, I founded Hertza Telecom, an internet service provider. Later, I founded a national telecommunications company. Today, I run ZeroBounce, an email validation and deliverability company I launched in a market already crowded with established competitors.

Every time I’ve started a new business, I’ve faced the same challenge: Why should anyone trust a company they’ve never heard of?

You can tout the quality of your product and its reliability all you want. You can use words like “leading” or “best-in-class” on your social media and website. But as it’s commonly said: talk is cheap. You may know your claims are true, but how do you get someone else to believe them?

It starts with a product that keeps its promises, so well that customers are willing to vouch for you. To reach the next level, you need credible third parties to back you up, too. Once you have all this, you have to raise your visibility.

None of this is easy, and you can’t skip any steps. Here’s what’s worked for me, from building a product people recommend to earning the kind of credibility you can’t buy.

Advertising can buy you short-term attention, but a product won’t last long if customers don’t like it or find it useful. If what you offer has serious flaws, word will spread fast.

Here’s the thing: Most founders get this backward. We think about the launch, the website, advertising, PR and growth long before the product lives up to its promises.

At ZeroBounce, accuracy was the promise everything else depended on. Before we launched, I wanted our email list validation service to reach at least 98% accuracy. It took a lot of testing and plenty of frustrating moments to get there.

When we launched, the website wasn’t pretty, and the back end left a lot to be desired. But the product was something we could stand behind. We’ve kept raising the bar since then. Today, we guarantee 99.6% email verification accuracy on most email domains, and we’ve published terms for what happens if we fall short. Your most important claims should be specific, because they need to be measurable.

Reviews have never been more valuable. We read them before booking a hotel room, ordering virtually any product under the sun and choosing software. Your customers are doing the same research on you. Don’t fear reviews. Embrace them and make them part of your marketing.

A good review can answer questions your website can’t. Did the product work well? Was support helpful? Did the customer say that they’d choose the product again?

But here’s what takes many founders a long time to learn: Handling praise is easy. Negative reviews are where you have a chance to shine.

That surprises some people. But how you respond when something goes wrong can say more than the review itself. We’ve had upset customers update a one-star review to five stars after seeing our genuine efforts to fix the problem.

Give your satisfied customers a frictionless way to share their experience, and do this early. Pay close attention to what people are saying, especially when the feedback is uncomfortable. Take your ego out of the equation. It isn’t easy, but that feedback is the most valuable information you have for improving your product. You’re also building a public record of how your company treats people.

Some customers will be unfair. That’s okay. You and your team can show true integrity.

Any company with a budget can throw money at advertising. PR is a different game. To make the news, an editor or producer has to decide you’re newsworthy and that their audience would care. You can’t pay for that. You have to earn it.

ZeroBounce has invested heavily in marketing over the years, but PR builds our credibility in a different way. When a renowned media organization features your company, the message packs a powerful punch because you can’t pay for it.

The same goes for industry awards and certifications. Security is a big deal for data companies like ours, so we complete annual SOC 2 Type 2 audits and hold ISO/IEC 27001 certification. We’ve also been recognized on national lists of the most successful companies in the U.S.

The point isn’t to collect media and award logos. It’s that there’s tremendous value when a credible organization examines part of your business and puts its own reputation on the line by praising your work.

You can’t assume a great product will find its market on its own.

We’ve tested various marketing channels at ZeroBounce because I wanted potential customers to find us wherever they were looking for a solution to their email marketing problems.

Say a prospect first reads an article about your company. Next, they see your name in search results. Then they visit your website, read customer reviews and look at your social media profiles. People rarely make an important business decision or a significant purchase after one exposure to a company. They research, compare and check the temperature before they decide.

What they’re looking for is consistency across all of those signals. They want to see satisfied customers and signs of trustworthy leadership. You’d be surprised how many online companies don’t have a single person’s name attached to them. You need an active presence and consistent information. Every box you check removes a little more uncertainty and earns a little more trust.

If someone hears about your company today, they may check out your company’s LinkedIn before they ever speak with your sales team. They’ll notice the language you use to describe the business, the kind of people who work there and what you publish. They’ll also notice whether customers engage with you and whether the company seems active. Have you ever visited a company’s LinkedIn page and found that its last post was a year and a half ago? What impression does that leave with you?

For B2B businesses especially, founders should give that presence the attention it deserves. We’ve built ZeroBounce’s presence across all major social media platforms. But two to three years ago, we looked closer at our metrics and we realized LinkedIn is where we should put most of our focus.

Putting our time and attention into LinkedIn has paid off: our community and engagement began to grow, and now we’re exploring new ways to reach more people. Our next step is to upgrade to a Premium Company Page.

The credibility features caught my attention. A LinkedIn Premium Company Page would let us feature a customer testimonial prominently and showcase our awards, right where prospects are already checking us out. When people like or comment on our posts, we could automatically invite them to follow the page. We’d also get deeper insight into how people engage with our content and how our page compares with competitors’.

That last part especially interests me — I want to know what catches people’s attention and where we stand against other companies in our space.

At a certain point, your company may pursue a higher-tier customer, enter into a new market, seek investors or become part of an acquisition. When that happens, the scrutiny is dialed up even more.

Decision makers will examine your product, customers and revenue. Everything will get a close look: your leadership, security, reviews, press coverage and how you’ve presented yourself through the years. Many companies try to polish these things right when they need them, when, in reality, their reputation should have been years in the making.

Start with building a product or service that’s worth trusting. Take the very best care of your customers. And let those customers speak. Give credible third parties plenty of reasons to talk about you. Market the business enough that the right people know it exists. And take care with every place a customer might go to look you up.

Trust takes time to build, but you don’t have to figure it out alone. LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build credibility and reach customers, and LinkedIn’s small business tools can help you strengthen every place prospects look you up.

You don’t need everyone to trust your company. You just need to give the right people enough good reasons to decide that they can.

I’ve been building technology companies for more than two decades.

When I started my first business at 18, selling computers in Romania, my “brand” was nonexistent. Like any entrepreneur starting out, I had to convince people to take a chance on a company they didn’t know. That’s far from easy.

In 2003, I founded Hertza Telecom, an internet service provider. Later, I founded a national telecommunications company. Today, I run ZeroBounce, an email validation and deliverability company I launched in a market already crowded with established competitors.

#5325. Bitcoin Price Holds $64K Ahead of Nvidia Earnings: AI Bubble Finally Pops?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price is struggling to find direction just below $65,000 as we brace for Nvidia earnings report. BTC USD has recovered from its weekend low near $62,000, but remains down 13% over seven days. Its modest rebound comes as technology stocks face yet another selling pressure.

This timing puts the Bitcoin price in an uncomfortable position. Nvidia’s results could determine if investors return to risk assets or abandon another crowded trade. With market sentiment still deep in extreme fear, we still have little conviction that the worst is over.

Meanwhile, Michael Burry is increasing his bearish bets against technology stocks. The investor made famous by The Big Short is targeting the Nasdaq-100 and semiconductor sector. His positioning raises an ugly question: Is the AI boom approaching its own dot-com moment?

Burry doubled his Nasdaq-100 put position on November 12, targeting early 2027 options 20% below the index’s market level. He also bought back part of his previously reduced bearish position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF.

His argument goes beyond stretched stock valuations. Burry believes conventional accounting earnings can exaggerate technology companies’ underlying profitability. Depreciation schedules, particularly across expensive data-center infrastructure, sit at the center of his concerns.

Consider a hyperscaler investing billions in GPUs and AI infrastructure. Those purchases become capital assets rather than immediate operating expenses. Companies subsequently recognize depreciation across their estimated useful lives.

This accounting treatment can make current earnings look stronger than the underlying cash economics. If hardware becomes obsolete faster than expected, reported profitability could overstate actual investment returns.

The concern becomes significant when companies must continuously replace expensive accelerators. Their infrastructure spending needs to generate sufficient revenue before the equipment loses economic value.

Burry isn’t alone in questioning the investment cycle. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previously acknowledged excessive enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence.

“Are we in a phase where investors as a whole are overexcited about AI? My opinion is yes,” Altman said.

Jeff Bezos offered another interpretation, describing the spending cycle as an “industrial bubble.” He argued that excessive investment could still produce valuable infrastructure, even when individual investors lose money.

Nvidia’s own Jensen Huang previously defended the industry’s economics. According to him, the AI infrastructure was already generating productive revenue, rather than merely attracting speculative capital.

The disagreement exposes the central tension surrounding the AI bubble. Demand can be genuine while valuations and infrastructure commitments become unsustainable.

The dot-com crash offers an important historical comparison. The Nasdaq Composite lost 78% between March 2000 and October 2002. Internet technology survived, but countless businesses and investors did not.

Today’s AI infrastructure market has similarities, particularly aggressive capital expenditure and expectations of exponential demand. However, established hyperscalers now finance much of the expansion through enormous operating businesses.

Now, can future AI revenue justify today’s investment?

Bitcoin once traded with relatively little correlation to traditional equities. That relationship changed dramatically as institutional participation expanded.

CME Group’s historical correlation research illustrates the shift. Between 2014 and 2016, Bitcoin’s correlation with the S&P 500 stood near -0.01. Its correlation with the Nasdaq-100 was effectively zero. Between 2020 and 2022, those correlations climbed to 0.40 and 0.42, respectively. They remained positive through April 2025, reaching 0.30 against both indices.

The shift matters because institutional investors increasingly treat Bitcoin as another liquid risk asset. Portfolio rebalancing, leveraged positions, and macroeconomic conditions can influence its price alongside technology stocks.

An AI sell-off could create another liquidity shock across crypto. Investors facing losses elsewhere might sell Bitcoin to raise cash or reduce overall exposure. But an AI correction doesn’t automatically invalidate Bitcoin’s monetary thesis. A technology valuation reset could eventually redirect capital toward alternative assets.

The gap lies between an isolated technology correction and a financial liquidity crisis. Bitcoin could eventually decouple from semiconductor stocks under the first scenario. The second could pressure both markets simultaneously. For now, Bitcoin price remains exposed to the same risk appetite driving technology shares.

Nvidia’s third-quarter fiscal 2027 results arrive at a particularly sensitive moment. Wall Street expects $109 billion in revenue and $2.47 in adjusted earnings per share.

Investors will focus heavily on Data Center revenue, gross margins, and forward guidance. The company’s Vera Rubin platform also faces scrutiny as customers expand their AI infrastructure commitments.

A headline earnings beat might not satisfy investors demanding another acceleration in growth. Strong revenue accompanied by cautious guidance could trigger another sell-the-news reaction.

The opposite scenario could restore confidence across technology stocks. Strong guidance would reinforce expectations that hyperscaler spending remains sustainable. Bitcoin could benefit if investors regain their appetite for speculative assets.

Technically, Bitcoin needs to stabilize above its recent $62,000 weekend low. A break below that level would expose the psychologically important $60,000 threshold.

A stronger recovery would put $68,000 back into view as an important technical resistance area. Reclaiming that level could help establish if buyers are returning.

Bitcoin price now faces a test extending beyond crypto markets. Nvidia must demonstrate that AI infrastructure spending can translate into durable earnings growth.

Burry is betting that expectations have run too far ahead. Huang’s former company built the infrastructure powering the AI revolution, but investors now need proof of its economic returns.

If the AI bubble starts deflating, Bitcoin must answer another question: Can it survive without Wall Street’s appetite for technology risk?

#5324. AI's one-model era is over

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Businesses stopped picking one AI. That’s a problem for the companies selling them, a threat that comes even as Anthropic is about to IPO

Photo Illustration by Cheng Xin/Getty Images

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s AI & Tech newsletter. Sign up here to get the latest AI & tech news, analysis and insights straight to your inbox.

Anthropic is days away from asking the public to buy in. Investors are weighing a pitch that values the Claude maker at up to $1.4 trillion, and Thursday is the expected first day of trading.

Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz.

That price assumes customers who picked Claude will keep picking Claude. But by the time the IPO roadshow started, many of them were already shopping around.

AT&T $T was one of them. In May, open models handled about a fifth of the telecom company’s AI work. By September, the share had doubled to 40%, and its AI costs had fallen by as much as 80% since earlier in the year.

The company did not drop Claude or ChatGPT. Instead, a router scored each request for difficulty, sent the easy ones to open models from Meta $META, Google $GOOGL, and Nvidia $NVDA, and saved the expensive models for the hard problems.

Revolut went further. The British fintech rolled out Claude Code in early 2026, and watched some engineers burn through up to $10,000 a month before capping their budgets.

Then it moved roughly 2,000 engineers onto GLM, an open-weight model from the Chinese developer Z.ai, running on 56 Nvidia chips operated in-house. The switch cut coding costs by about 90% in under a year.

They are not the only ones being a little promiscuous. On Vercel’s AI Gateway, a service that lets developers access models from many providers through one connection, almost a third of teams changed their most-used provider in September alone.

Open-weight models handled 71.5% of traffic that month and captured almost a quarter of spending, up from about one-twentieth in June.

The growing competition put pressure on prices, even as more tokens are used. Spending through the gateway ran about 13 times higher than in December 2025, while the average price per token dropped 47%.

The consumer data offered another warning for the model makers. As providers' capabilities expanded, consumers became less likely to pay for multiple services at once. They were switching between providers, but increasingly saw little reason to pay for more than one. People were dating around, one subscription at a time.

For the giants, this is an awkward moment to discover how little loyalty their customers owed them. Anthropic has committed close to $900 billion to data center capacity, much of it through long-term agreements that would be difficult to unwind. Its third-quarter operating loss was $567 million. The economics depend on keeping customers willing to pay a premium for its models.

Fortunately for Anthropic, it still led where the money was. Claude Opus 5.5 took 11% of September spending on Vercel’s gateway, more than double the share of OpenAI’s top model, which came in second. A Chinese model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, ranked third.

The shift also created opportunities for the middlemen, as it tends to in a gold rush. Gateways and routers were becoming the point where customers chose between models, while American hosting providers collected more than two-thirds of the September spending on Chinese models.

None of it should have come as a surprise. A Google researcher had laid out the whole problem in an internal memo that escaped onto a public Discord server in 2023. They argued that neither their employer nor OpenAI had a moat, and that customers would stop paying for a model once a free one was nearly as good.

Anthropic’s prospectus ran to more than 400 pages. While it never used the word moat, its risk factors warned that customers might drift toward “smaller, cheaper, or open-source alternatives.”

#5323. Early data points to Vulcan’s first stage in launch failure that cost Amazon 40 Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday.

In its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

That stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA said it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA said. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

ULA said Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based company hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and New Glenn for our return to flight.”

Impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on New Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight.

Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

Amazon has said it plans to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

#5322. Big Sean and Jalen Rose made it big. Now they’re making sure they keep showing up for the city that raised them

For the 13th draft pick Jalen Rose, loving Detroit means showing up for the city on the good days, the bad days, and all the ordinary ones in between. The former NBA star—whose mother created the name Jalen—has spent years giving back to the place that raised him. And along the way, he’s learned what separates those who lift Detroit from those who only show up during election time.

“You show up during a holiday or election, that type of thing, but you’re not here on a Wednesday when it’s the middle of January and it’s freezing outside,” Rose said Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

Sitting beside him was multi-platinum rapper Big Sean, whose real name is Sean Michael Leonard Anderson, who also grew up in Detroit and has turned his success into opportunities for young people back home. Between Rose’s tuition-free high school, Big Sean’s recording studios, and their growing entertainment ventures, the two are investing in Detroit’s next generation while trying to make the city a place where young talent can build careers of their own.

Rose understands firsthand what it means to grow up without much. Some days, his family didn’t have heat or hot water, so they relied on kerosene heaters and boiled water to wash.

“My motivation was growing up poor and watching, you know, my mother go to work,” he said.

As a kid, he promised his mother he’d make it to the NBA and get their family out of poverty. He even started writing “Dr. J” on his school papers, borrowing the nickname of the basketball legend Julius Erving.

“I’m going to the league. You know, I’m gonna get us out the hood,” he recalled telling her. He kept that promise, playing 13 seasons in the NBA and never forgetting the people who helped him get there.

Now, his Jalen Rose Leadership Academy is completing its 16th school year, serving 460 high school students and supporting roughly 1,100 graduates pursuing education after high school, Rose said. And the work is paying off, as Rose noted that the school has Detroit’s highest student index, a distinction he takes immense pride in.

And Big Sean has been in Rose’s corner since long before they shared a stage Tuesday, attending the academy’s first graduation back in 2015. More than a decade later, the students keep Rose motivated.

“You know, our young people, the way they receive it just makes me want to work harder for them because they deserve the opportunities,” Rose said.

Giving back started long before Big Sean went platinum with hits like “Blessings” and “Bounce Back.”

His grandmother served as a captain in the Six Triple Eight, the all-Black, all-female Army unit that sorted military mail during World War II. Growing up, he watched her make helping others a family tradition, no matter how much the family had.

“No matter how good or bad the years were,” Big Sean recalled, his grandmother made sure the family donated clothes and supported people in need—a lesson that stayed with him as his music career took him around the world.

The Sean Anderson Foundation is run by his mother, who was backstage Tuesday while his father and brother cheered from the audience. Through it, he has built recording studios at Boys & Girls Clubs, giving young people a chance to learn not only how to perform but also how to become sound engineers and work behind the scenes.

The first of those studios opened at his alma mater, Cass Technical High School, where Big Sean once risked suspension for selling his own CDs. Years later, he had his own kind of “Bounce Back” moment, returning to the school not to sell music, but to help the next generation make it.

“It was cool to see a full-circle 180 moment,” he said.

The work has since expanded to the new Boys & Girls Club at Detroit’s restored Michigan Central Station, where he and Usher backed the $1 million Detroit Entertainment Innovation Incubator, which opened in February, to give young Detroiters access to creative and technical training.

There, young people can explore everything from engineering and film makeup to sneaker resale and tech. Big Sean said seeing young people from those programs land jobs has been one of the most rewarding experiences of his career.

“It’s the first time that I’ve seen all the hard work of giving back starting to pay off,” he said.

Both men are also thinking beyond philanthropy, working to make Detroit a place where creative talent can build careers—not just a place artists leave once they get noticed.

Rose launched Same Page Entertainment in February with Detroit Pistons owner Tom Gores, aiming to produce films, documentaries, television shows, and other media from Detroit.

He said the goal is to create the kind of entertainment hub Tyler Perry built in Atlanta, giving Detroiters opportunities both in front of and behind the camera. For years, Rose said, pursuing a media career meant leaving Detroit for Los Angeles or New York. He wants to change that.

Big Sean, who also sees some NBA crossover serving as the Pistons’ creative director of global experience, has been using the team’s platform to spotlight local artists. He even teased a major entertainment project that he said Michigan Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson knows about and wants to support, though he wasn’t ready to announce details just yet.

“Detroit has something magical here, and it’s up to us to activate the magic,” Big Sean said.

And even as his career has taken him around the world, he hasn’t forgotten where it all started. He sees his success as a chance to make the road a little easier for those coming after him.

“Wherever we go, you always leave breadcrumbs behind,” he said, explaining that those breadcrumbs aren’t just for finding his own way home, but for helping someone else follow the path.

#5320. How to Spot Employee Burnout Before the Holiday Rush Takes Its Toll

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Here’s how small businesses can use workforce technology to prevent employee burnout and keep operations running smoothly.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For a small business owner, a perfectly planned holiday schedule can bring a sigh of relief. Every shift is covered, employees are picking up extra hours, and the team is poised to keep pace with demand. But a schedule that works on paper can hide a business that is leaning too heavily on the same people.

Your most dependable employee may be covering their third extra shift this week. A manager may be staying late every day to finish work that customer demands pushed aside. Those efforts keep the business moving today, but relying on them week after week, especially at a small or growing business, leaves little room for employees to recover or for the business to handle another absence.

That is why burnout prevention belongs in holiday business planning and workforce strategy. Burnout is often treated as an employee well-being issue, but for small businesses it is also an operational challenge. When fatigue, overtime, absenteeism and scheduling pressure build across a workforce, they create risks that affect service levels, productivity and the ability to meet customer demand.

The right workforce technology helps owners see that pressure building. Connecting scheduling, timekeeping and payroll information makes it possible to spot recurring workload problems, understand who is affected and adjust coverage before another request to stay late becomes the only solution.

UKG’s 2025 Retail Workforce Report found that only 18% of retailers anticipated employee burnout as a major challenge. Meanwhile, UKG’s 2025 global study of frontline workers found that 76% of frontline employees reported feeling burned out at work.

Underestimating that strain can lead an owner to plan for holiday sales the team cannot sustainably support. If the staffing plan assumes everyone can keep adding hours, a single absence can leave the business struggling to serve customers and put even more pressure on the people who remain. Earlier visibility into workload gives owners time to arrange coverage before that cycle begins.

Small business leaders often work alongside their employees and know them well. Yet familiarity can make a staffing problem harder to recognize. The person who always volunteers becomes the first person asked, and a supervisor’s willingness to stay late gradually becomes part of the plan.

Disconnected systems make that pattern easier to miss. A schedule shows a filled shift, while payroll records the extra hours after they have been worked. Bringing those records together gives owners a clearer view of how often the business depends on the same employees to close its staffing gaps.

Overtime is one of the most important workforce operations signals because it shows where demand and workforce capacity are no longer aligned. Occasional extra hours may be welcome for some, but repeated overtime concentrated among a few employees warrants a closer look, especially when their schedules also leave little time between shifts.

Imagine a small retailer whose most experienced associate regularly stays an hour past her scheduled finish. Each request seems reasonable in isolation. Over three weeks, however, she also covers two absences and works several closing shifts followed by early openings. The owner sees someone dependable; the combined records reveal the true cost of how much additional work she is carrying.

Connected timekeeping and scheduling tools can make that cumulative demand visible without requiring the owner to reconstruct it from old schedules and messages. Alerts about approaching overtime or short intervals between shifts give a manager a chance to discuss coverage before publishing the next schedule.

Attendance changes add another piece of context. If absences rise on a team that has been working extra hours, the combination is worth exploring. While data alone does not establish that someone is burned out, it helps managers ask better questions about workload and support.

This is where workforce analytics earns its value for a lean business: It helps owners manage workforce operations proactively rather than reactively. Effective workforce operations requires connecting labor demand, staffing levels, scheduling, attendance, timekeeping and employee experience data to create a complete picture of how work gets done. When leaders can see those connections, they can intervene before a staffing challenge becomes an operational disruption.

Holiday staffing decisions often start with last year’s sales, but sales alone cannot explain why a team keeps falling behind. A store may have enough labor hours for the week and still depend on employees staying late because coverage does not line up with the work. That mismatch can turn an otherwise manageable holiday workload into a recurring source of exhaustion.

Consider a shop where afternoon pickup orders regularly arrive while employees are unloading a delivery. Associates leave stocking unfinished to help customers, then spend the end of their shifts catching up. To an owner reviewing weekly totals, the overtime may suggest the store simply needs more hours overall. Connecting order activity, labor demand, scheduling and timekeeping data can reveal a workforce operations problem that would otherwise remain hidden.

With demand forecasting and scheduling technology, that pattern can inform the next schedule. If the overlap is likely to recur, the manager can plan for stockroom coverage while keeping associates available to serve customers. AI-assisted scheduling can help identify an employee with the right skills and availability, reducing the time the manager spends working through possible changes.

The benefit is that the closing team no longer has to absorb the same unfinished work night after night. Addressing the bottleneck earlier can make finishing on time more predictable, giving employees greater confidence in their schedules. For the owner, it also creates a clearer basis for deciding whether to move existing coverage or invest in additional hours.

Better data also makes employee conversations more useful. A manager who can see repeated extra shifts can ask how that arrangement is working and what would make the coming weeks manageable. The answer may be a consistent day off, a different start time or continued access to additional hours.

That distinction matters during a season when employees may be balancing holiday expenses with family responsibilities. An automatic reduction in hours could create a different source of stress. Current availability and employee preferences help managers respond to what people actually need.

In UKG’s 2025 retail survey, 86% of retailers said frontline employees wanted more flexibility than their organizations provided. For small businesses, delivering that flexibility can be difficult when every change requires phone calls, group texts and a manager to coordinate the exchange.

Mobile self-service scheduling reduces that friction by letting employees view schedules, request time off and arrange shift swaps in one place. Scheduling rules can help check that replacement coverage meets role requirements and flag potential overtime. Employees gain a practical way to manage a conflict, while managers spend less time chasing responses.

The benefit goes beyond convenience. Someone who can resolve a scheduling conflict has more control over how work fits into life outside it. When employees see that technology makes those adjustments easier, they have a concrete reason to trust its role in the workplace.

Small businesses rarely have someone available to spend hours analyzing workforce reports. Technology is more useful when it brings a developing problem to the manager’s attention and makes the next decision easier, such as highlighting an open shift alongside qualified employees who are available to work.

Timing determines how many options remain. A coverage gap identified before next week’s schedule is published may be addressed through a voluntary shift change or additional staffing. The same gap discovered during a rush is more likely to land on whoever is already there.

Managers need that support themselves. UKG’s retail report found that 31% of retailers said managers worked additional shifts when understaffed. A supervisor covering the floor has less time to plan coverage or help a new employee learn the job, which can leave the team dependent on the same experienced people again.

Keeping demand forecasts and schedules connected also matters after peak sales pass. Returns and inventory work can continue into January, and a smaller team may still face a substantial workload. Visibility into that work gives owners a better basis for deciding when staffing can ease.

A successful holiday season depends on having a workforce that can sustain the work and the operational visibility to support it. Burnout, absenteeism, overtime, scheduling conflicts and staffing shortages are often treated as separate challenges, but they are all connected workforce operations signals.

When small businesses bring those signals together, they gain a clearer understanding of how work gets done across the organization. Workforce operations technology provides the visibility needed to identify strain early, align staffing with demand and respond before employee pressure becomes an operational problem.

Ultimately, organizations that manage workforce operations effectively are better positioned to support their people, serve customers consistently and perform through the busiest times of the year.

For a small business owner, a perfectly planned holiday schedule can bring a sigh of relief. Every shift is covered, employees are picking up extra hours, and the team is poised to keep pace with demand. But a schedule that works on paper can hide a business that is leaning too heavily on the same people.

Your most dependable employee may be covering their third extra shift this week. A manager may be staying late every day to finish work that customer demands pushed aside. Those efforts keep the business moving today, but relying on them week after week, especially at a small or growing business, leaves little room for employees to recover or for the business to handle another absence.

That is why burnout prevention belongs in holiday business planning and workforce strategy. Burnout is often treated as an employee well-being issue, but for small businesses it is also an operational challenge. When fatigue, overtime, absenteeism and scheduling pressure build across a workforce, they create risks that affect service levels, productivity and the ability to meet customer demand.

#5319. Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share, giving it a $1.5 trillion valuation

Anthropic priced shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday at $83 per share, above its initially guided ranged of $70 to $78 per share, and likely valuing the AI company at $1.5 trillion.

Anthropic’s stock will begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker ANT, marking one of the most highly anticipated IPOs in years as well as one of the largest ever.

The San Francisco-based AI company said it increased the number of shares sold in the offering to 980 million, instead of the 825 million shares it initially planned to sell. The expanded float means Anthropic will raise roughly $80 billion in the IPO—and as much as $92 billion if the underwriters choose to exercise an over-allotment option.

The offering will provide Anthropic with a critical infusion of capital as it seeks to stay ahead in the AI race and to invest in the computing infrastructure to train its models. The IPO will also make instant billionaires out of numerous Anthropic employees and early investors, particularly the seven cofounders who created Anthropic in San Francisco just five years ago.

Anthropic is the first pure-play maker of frontier AI models to go public (SpaceX also does rockets, and Google and Meta both have massive businesses in search and social media), and its Wall Street debut is being closely watched as a barometer for the health of the broader AI industry. The IPO comes as the AI boom is in a period of uncertainty following a leadership shake up at AI chipmaker Nvidia and growing public backlash to AI data centers.

At a $1.5 trillion valuation, Anthropic would be the second most valuable IPO of all time, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO in June. Measured by capital raised however, Anthropic’s $80 billion would top the $75 billon raised by SpaceX.

Seven strategic partners, including Google and Nvidia, have also agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting Anthropic stock at the IPO price.

Anthropic’s revenue has soared thanks to strong demand from business customers. In the nine months ending September 30, Anthropic generated $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. The company posted a $104 billion net loss in its most recent nine-month period, though the bulk of the red ink is because of the way it accounted for its convertible notes.

#5318. Seattle tech vet and Sounders FC minority owner Chee Chew joins front office to lead AI push

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am

Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a new job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.

“His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer said in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation company toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

Chew said his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

“In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”

Chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he said. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said.

The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he said.

Talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years. It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and said, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew says he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he said. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

He recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew said, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew said he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

The bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew said. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

“It has to be approachable for folks,” he said. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”

The Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he said.

#5317. JPMorgan taps 20-year company veteran Bregje de Best as its next CFO

JPMorgan Chase has named Bregje de Best, who has spent two decades at the company, as its next chief financial officer.

The 43-year-old will lead the finance organization at JPMorgan Chase, No. 12 on the Fortune 500. The company had $5.1 trillion in assets and $372 billion in stockholders’ equity as of Sept. 30. She will succeed Jeremy Barnum following the company’s first-quarter 2027 financial reporting, JPMorgan announced Tuesday.

At that time, she will join the firm-wide operating committee, and Barnum will become a vice chairman. Barnum informed the company of his intention to conclude his tenure as CFO after six years in the role.

The appointment will make de Best the latest woman to serve as JPMorgan’s CFO. Her predecessors include Marianne Lake, who held the role from 2013 to 2019, and Jennifer Piepszak, now chief operating officer, who served as CFO from 2019 to 2021.

Since June 2025, de Best has served as CFO of JPMorgan’s commercial and investment bank (CIB). The Dutch banker joined the company in 2006 and previously served as co-head of global corporate banking. DeBest has also held senior roles in investment banking and markets in the United Kingdom and Asia.

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon described de Best in the announcement as an “extraordinary leader,” citing her experience in finance and across the CIB’s businesses. “She has a deep understanding of how our company operates,” Dimon said.

Her investment banking background is shared by a notable number of current CFOs. According to executive search firm Crist Kolder Associates’ 2026 midyear Volatility Report, 22% of sitting CFOs at companies in its combined Fortune 500 and S&P 500 sample have investment banking experience. Of those with that background, 20% work in the financial industry.

Research also finds that companies increasingly want CFOs with operational experience. De Best’s experience extends to the operational side of the business: As CIB CFO, she oversees business management and controls across JPMorgan’s global banking, markets, payments and securities services businesses.

In a LinkedIn post earlier this year, de Best described attending a firm-wide senior leadership conference focused on resilience, global growth and the rapid pace of innovation. “It’s clear that AI and digital assets are transforming every aspect of our business, and I’m energized by our commitment to building for the future and leading the industry forward,” she wrote.

Barnum and de Best will work closely during the transition. He will lead the January and April earnings announcements and the company’s Investor Day in February, according to JPMorgan. After becoming a vice chairman following first-quarter reporting, he will remain at the company until early 2028, working with Dimon and other senior leaders on firm-wide initiatives.

The company will announce de Best’s successor as CFO of the CIB early next year.

Sheryl Estrada is a senior writer at Fortune, where she covers the corporate finance industry, Wall Street, and corporate leadership. She also authors CFO Daily.

#5316. The Rooms Where AI Gets Decided Are Filling Up. Women Need to Be in Them

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is redrawing the path to leadership within companies, and women risk being left out. Proximity to the AI strategy, governance, and operating decisions that guide the next generation of enterprise leadership is critical for women looking to grow their career, expand their role, or become leaders in their organization.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

AI is one of the biggest market-moving shifts we have ever seen. Leaders are reorganizing around the technology, new businesses are being built around the opportunity, and decisions being made about AI today will define our economy for generations.

I care passionately about seeing more women in leadership, having access to capital, and steering the choices that shape our world. So when I heard AI expert and advisor Allie K. Miller on Emma Grede’s podcast share that women were adopting AI 25% less than men, it stuck with me.

For my whole career, I’ve watched women start a step behind: we still hold only about 29% of C-suite roles and make up fewer than one in five decision-makers at venture firms. Even 2025, a banner year for women-founded startups, tells a misleading story: nearly 41% of the almost $74 billion raised came from two megadeals. Most women founders saw very few of those investment dollars.If women are already underrepresented among leaders, investors, and founders, and now we’re adopting AI more slowly, the gap widens at the exact moment the next generation of business leaders and global decision-makers are being decided.

Concerns around whether AI is ethical or looks like cheating are driving women’s slower adoption, but I also think it comes down to time. We badly underestimate what it takes to carve out hours to learn something new on top of a full-time job, personal responsibilities, and commitments to friends and loved ones. If I spend a Sunday afternoon building an agent, I’m missing time with my family. The trade-offs are real, and you don’t get that time back.

Research suggests the adoption gap may be shrinking, but given how fast AI is moving, incremental progress is not enough. This isn’t a shift women can opt out of. If we want to drive the decisions that will define the next decade, we need to be leading this transformation, not watch it unfold.Here are four things I believe women should focus on right now:

I always come back to this line from Ginni Rometty: growth and comfort do not coexist.I’ve seen this firsthand throughout my career: I joined ServiceNow just before COVID hit. Within ten weeks, I went from never having worked from home to doing everything remotely—building relationships, leading a team, and learning dozens of new tools. It wasn’t comfortable, but my team and I adapted. AI demands the same mindset.

The women I see pulling ahead here are the ones who just start using AI before they feel ready or have it all figured out. Getting your hands dirty is the whole point: use AI to analyze a dense report, pressure-test a strategy, or build a simple agent to handle a task you dislike.Pick low-risk moments and let yourself get things wrong. You learn AI by being close to it, not by watching from a distance and waiting until you feel like an expert.

You don’t have to navigate this shift alone. Seek out AI-specific meetups and groups—and connect with professionals who are experimenting in real time and asking the same questions as you.

It is also worth looking closer to home. Some of our best AI teachers at ServiceNow have been early-career employees who are more comfortable with these tools than others. A little reverse mentoring can go a long way.

Just as importantly, you need to pay it forward. The more women help each other build confidence and capability around AI, the faster we will close the gap. One of the reasons we invited Allie K. Miller to talk about AI and leadership at Knowledge, our annual conference, is that she consistently shares insights that lower the barrier to entry for others.

You can’t be what you can’t see, which is why those of us in senior leadership roles also need to lead by example. When I’m asked how I use AI as a CFO, I’m deliberate about sharing how it has become a real partner in how I work. I want women coming up behind me to see AI fluency as part of their own leadership path, too.

For much of my career, I was the only woman with a seat at the table. Looking back, I can see how much that proximity shaped my career. Watching leaders like Barry Diller and Dara Khosrowshahi navigate complex, high-stakes decisions taught me lessons no class ever could.It also gave me exposure to projects that prepared me to lead. Before IAC, I didn’t have much M&A experience. There, I learned what a good deal actually looks like, how to think about integration, and the kind of judgment you can only build by doing the work.

The same principle applies to women and AI right now. Get as close to the AI decision-making as possible. Participate in strategy conversations, use-case assessments, pilots, and learning sessions. Raise your hand for the AI project no one has figured out yet and ask to be in the room where your company is determining how it will use this technology.

When leadership sees you leaning into the hardest, most important work the company is taking on, you become someone they picture in the next big role.

Understand Your Role in the AI TransformationWe need more than just engineers and programmers working closely with AI.

To ensure artificial intelligence is as safe, ethical, and effective as it can be, we need people with diverse perspectives and skills working on it. Those with expertise in governance, risk, talent, and change management, for example, have important roles to play in ensuring successful AI deployment at scale.

At ServiceNow, when we added “AI Enablement” to Jacqui Canney’s title of Chief People Officer, it was done for a reason. AI can’t just be dropped into the tooling mix. People need to understand and learn how to use it well in the enterprise, which means we need to invest in that happening.

We’ve done this in many ways, from company-wide learning sessions, to role-based skills development opportunities through ServiceNow University, to building groups of AI champions that shape how the technology is being used at the team level.

Even the best company programs won’t do it all for you, though. I always say that no one will care as much about your career as you do, and that’s to no fault of your managers or your company. They may open doors, but you’re the one who must walk through them.

The rooms where AI is being built, deployed, trained, and governed are filling up, and if you’re not in them, those decisions are getting made without you. The time you invest now in learning, the skills you build, and the judgment you develop will compound. As this next era of leadership unfolds, the women who stayed close to AI won’t just be ready for the future; they’ll help define it.

AI is one of the biggest market-moving shifts we have ever seen. Leaders are reorganizing around the technology, new businesses are being built around the opportunity, and decisions being made about AI today will define our economy for generations.

I care passionately about seeing more women in leadership, having access to capital, and steering the choices that shape our world. So when I heard AI expert and advisor Allie K. Miller on Emma Grede’s podcast share that women were adopting AI 25% less than men, it stuck with me.

For my whole career, I’ve watched women start a step behind: we still hold only about 29% of C-suite roles and make up fewer than one in five decision-makers at venture firms. Even 2025, a banner year for women-founded startups, tells a misleading story: nearly 41% of the almost $74 billion raised came from two megadeals. Most women founders saw very few of those investment dollars.If women are already underrepresented among leaders, investors, and founders, and now we’re adopting AI more slowly, the gap widens at the exact moment the next generation of business leaders and global decision-makers are being decided.

#5315. Seattle police unleash dog-like robot whose best trick is bomb dispoal

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am

Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

It’s a big upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD said a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

The only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the company’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

Police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. New York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

Back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a new name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”

#5314. Microsoft jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, touting cheaper, customizable AI models of its own

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” said Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the company’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he said.

The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou said.

Microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” users of each company’s agent tools, it showed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

Partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

The companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

New MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

The lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft says it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it says matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

The other new business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff showed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

The cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he said.

Microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A new Agent 365 Business Analytics feature shows business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

In another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.
